input:
Unplanned downtime remains a persistent and costly challenge for the plant, and it is increasingly clear that a more proactive, data-driven approach to maintenance could play a pivotal role in addressing it. This memo explores the potential opportunity presented by condition-monitoring sensors, drawing on the plant's maintenance records, vendor information, and a proposed pilot programme, in order to support a well-informed decision at the March capital review.

According to the plant's maintenance records, which cover a period of 12 months and a total of 180 pumps, the plant experienced no less than 1291 h of unplanned downtime over the year. A closer analysis of these figures reveals that bearing failures account for 46% of the downtime hours, highlighting the fact that a single failure category is responsible for a substantial share of the total losses. Against this backdrop, a sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $433k installed, together with an ongoing cost of $79k per year. Encouragingly, in a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were able to cut downtime by 25%, although it should be noted that this 25% figure is a vendor figure and has not been measured at this plant.

It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so this aspect of maintenance planning would remain exactly as it is today. Weighing the costs and benefits together, a full installation would commit the plant to $433k up front plus $79k per year on the strength of an unverified vendor claim, whereas a more measured approach would be to run a three-month pilot on 16 pumps at a cost of $41k, allowing the effect to be measured on the plant's own equipment first. On balance, therefore, it is recommended that the three-month pilot, costing $41k in total, be approved, with the reliability engineering group owning the pilot and reporting its results before the March capital review, and with the decision on full installation held until those results are available.

The reliability engineering group recommends a three-month pilot of condition sensors on 16 pumps, at a cost of $41k, before any decision on plant-wide installation. Unplanned downtime is the loss under review. The plant record establishes the size of the loss but not the effect of the sensors, and the only effect figure available is the vendor's; the recommendation is a pilot for that reason. The decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported, ahead of the March capital review.

The case rests on the plant's own maintenance records. The records cover 12 months and all 180 pumps, and they show 1291 h of unplanned downtime. Bearing failures account for 46% of the downtime hours. The largest share of the plant's unplanned downtime therefore sits in a single failure class, and the pilot is directed at the downtime total that the records establish.

A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $433k installed, plus $79k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 25%. The 25% figure is a vendor figure; it was not measured at this plant, and no part of the recommendation rests on it.

The pilot commits $41k over three months against a full installation quoted at $433k plus $79k per year, and it returns a plant measurement in place of the vendor figure. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and the pilot does not alter them.

The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports its results before the March capital review. The full-installation decision is taken at that review, on the pilot results. A decision taken now would rest on the vendor figure. A decision taken at the review rests on a measurement made at the plant.
